clue.text: Hates lot being cut short: hates changes

indicators.note: something cut short loses its end, so the last letter of the word lot is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, before its tail is docked

indicators.note: the letters of the second hates change places and are rearranged into a new order

parts.note: the second hates is the anagram fodder, its five letters taken as written and then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone resents their allotment being trimmed, and resents any alteration too.
explanation.walkthrough: Reconstructed clue: the Guardian's text lost a word, so 'lot' is supplied to give the opening pair of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe is to detest intensely, a stronger synonym for hating something.

clue.text: Maybe Will left it

definitions.meaning: read as a man named Will, but really a last testament, of which this is one example
suggests someone departing, but means bequeathed in a testament

explanation.surface: It reads as though a man called Will may have abandoned something.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital W disguises a testament; what a testament leaves behind to heirs is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A legacy is money or property bequeathed to someone in a testament, exactly what such a document leaves.

clue.text: A plank on a ship

parts.note: taken as written
a plank is a long flat length of timber, also called a board

explanation.surface: A piece of timber found on a sailing vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Being aboard means being on or in a vessel, the usual word for passengers on a ship.

clue.text: Without leader, blew hot and cold before being restrained

indicators.note: the letters for hot and cold are placed in front of the shortened word

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a leader goes first, so the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: to blow is to puff, so blew gives puffed

explanation.surface: Someone who vacillated and dithered ends up shackled by the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blew hot and cold' looks like the idiom for wavering, but it splits into a verb and two tap abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Being handcuffed means having the wrists locked together, a literal form of physical restraint.

clue.text: Spell "wader"

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a period of time spent doing a job
second meaning: a small sandpiper of the shore, a bird that wades

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look like an instruction to spell out a word; instead the two words are separate meanings of one answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a fixed period of work and a small shorebird of the sandpiper family.

clue.text: Source of perfume becomes hip with age

definitions.meaning: a flower that will open into a fragrant bloom, the raw material of scent
sounds like growing fashionable in later life, but a rose's fruit is called a hip

explanation.surface: Something fragrant turns trendy as it gets older.
explanation.walkthrough: Hip is the botanical name for the fruit a rose forms once its flower fades.
explanation.definitionFit: An unopened rose flower gives scent when it blooms and later ripens into a rose hip.

clue.text: Mention politeness, if given new start

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word for politeness is swapped for a different one

parts.note: deference is respectful courtesy shown to someone

explanation.surface: Talk about good manners when it is refreshed.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letter D is replaced by R; the clue does not say which letter, so the definition decides it.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a reference to something is to mention or allude to it in passing.

clue.text: See 17
It might be funny to include short sermon on conviviality

indicators.note: the first word wraps round the shortened sermon

parts.note: the funny bone is the spot on the elbow, so this phrase gives that body part

indicators.note: the sermon word is cut short, losing its final two letters

parts.note: a homily is a short moralising sermon

explanation.surface: A brief jokey talk about good cheer might be amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: The funny bone is the elbow nerve; 'It might be funny' points to that particular bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonhomie is cheerful friendliness and good nature, a close match for conviviality at a gathering.

clue.text: Reading a novel, "A network of sewers"

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: the nine letters of these two words, taken as written, are the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone is reading a book whose title is A Network of Sewers.
explanation.definitionFit: Drainage is the system of pipes and channels that carries away waste water, a sewer network.

clue.text: Force horse to whimper

parts.note: G is the symbol for gravitational force, as in g-force
a roan is a horse whose coat is flecked with white

explanation.surface: Make a horse cry out by compelling it.
explanation.definitionFit: A groan is a low moan of pain or distress, close kin to a whimper.

clue.text: In New Zealand, a pipe is held to cause illness

indicators.note: the pipe is gripped inside the other letters

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a flue is a duct or pipe carrying smoke from a fire

explanation.surface: Someone in New Zealand gets sick from holding a pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: Influenza is the viral disease commonly called flu, a familiar seasonal illness.

clue.text: "Cook/Blair — the last two" — accurate satire

indicators.note: to cook figures is to falsify or rework them, so these letters are reorganised

parts.note: only the final pair of letters of the surname are used
taken as written: its eight letters join the pair from Blair as fodder

explanation.surface: A pointed jibe pairing two Labour politicians, Robin Cook and Tony Blair, is said to be spot-on mockery.
explanation.walkthrough: Cook looks like the politician but is the anagram signal; take the end of Blair and mix it with accurate.
explanation.definitionFit: A caricature is an exaggerated portrait made for comic or mocking effect, a form of satire.

clue.text: Drink on the floor

definitions.meaning: second meaning: fallen or knocked over

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a spilt drink; instead it is two separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for gulping a drink and an adverb for being flat on the ground.

clue.text: High excitement to go and get wriggling viper inside

indicators.note: the jumbled snake goes within the word for retrieving

parts.note: to fetch is to go and bring something back

indicators.note: a wriggling snake twists about, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the snake's name, taken as written, supplies the five letters to be jumbled

explanation.surface: A thrilling moment when someone must retrieve a writhing snake from within.
explanation.definitionFit: Fever pitch is a state of intense agitation or excitement, the peak of a crowd's frenzy.

clue.text: Fishing at sea?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, playful: catching a kind of flatfish
second meaning: confused and struggling, thrashing about

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a trawler; the question mark warns that the fishing sense is a joke on a flatfish name.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means struggling helplessly and, whimsically, angling for a particular flatfish.

clue.text: Watchful voters ban fraud

indicators.note: electoral fraud scrambles the result, so these letters are scrambled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written: these nine letters are the fodder

explanation.surface: Vigilant electors outlaw ballot-rigging.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone observant notices things readily and keeps a careful eye out, which is being alert.

clue.text: Fantastic novel, "About a Boy" (unfinished)

indicators.note: the new word goes around the other pieces, enclosing them

parts.note: novel and fresh both mean new and original
taken as written

indicators.note: the youngster's word is left incomplete, missing its final letter

parts.note: a kid is a child or youngster, such as a young lad

explanation.surface: An outlandish book called About a Boy, left incomplete; About a Boy is a novel by Nick Hornby.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hornby title is a red herring; About is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Freakish means bizarre and abnormal, close to fantastic in its sense of strange or unreal.

clue.text: Scorcese''s full version of "Head or Tail"?

parts.note: a director is the head of an organisation or board
a scut is the short upright tail of a rabbit, hare or deer

explanation.surface: Martin Scorsese's longer edition of a film titled Head or Tail.
explanation.walkthrough: Head and tail look like a coin toss, but each gives one word of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A film-maker's preferred edit, often longer than the cinema release, as Scorsese might restore.

clue.text: Lift blockade of Eire with assegai, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps marks the letters as one possible arrangement among many, so they are reordered

parts.note: the Irish name for Ireland, taken as written as part of the fodder
a Zulu spear, taken as written: its seven letters complete the fodder

explanation.surface: Relieve an Irish blockade using a Zulu spear, maybe; an assegai is a slender iron-tipped spear.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise a siege is to end the surrounding of a town, lifting the blockade around it.

clue.text: General takes Major's wife to port

parts.note: Norma Major is the wife of the former Prime Minister John Major
port is the left side of a ship, abbreviated L

explanation.surface: An army general escorts a major's spouse to a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: General and Major look like military ranks; Major is the prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: General and normal both describe what is usual or common to most cases.

clue.text: Penguin slime covering medical tubes?

indicators.note: the sticky stuff goes round and covers the other letters

parts.note: goo is sticky, slimy matter
ENT is ear, nose and throat medicine, a specialty of the body's passages

explanation.surface: A penguin's slime coats some tubes in a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that ear, nose and throat are only loosely tubes.
explanation.definitionFit: The gentoo is a species of penguin with a white stripe over its head, found in the Antarctic.

clue.text: Old painter to return shortly

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters are read in reverse
the artist's name is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: Edgar Degas was a French Impressionist painter

explanation.surface: An elderly artist will come back soon.
explanation.definitionFit: Aged means elderly, having lived a long time, a plain synonym for old.

clue.text: Player at Table 1 takes order back

indicators.note: takes means holds, so the chart word holds the reversed letters within it

parts.note: a graph, like a table, is a chart displaying data

indicators.note: read backwards, so the letters of the honour are reversed

parts.note: OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour
the numeral is spelt out as the word one

explanation.surface: A card player at the first table returns a command.
explanation.walkthrough: Player is a record player; Table and order are chart and honour.
explanation.definitionFit: A gramophone is an old record player, playing discs with a needle and horn.

clue.text: Michelin first to produce "A to Z of Food"

indicators.note: the first letter of the tyre maker's name is taken

parts.note: the tyre company's name supplies just its first letter

indicators.note: producing something new from these letters means rearranging them

parts.note: the four letters of this phrase, taken as written, are the fodder

explanation.surface: Michelin's guide begins by publishing a complete food guide.
explanation.definitionFit: Matzo is unleavened bread eaten at Passover, a particular kind of food.

clue.text: Formerly a roundabout

parts.note: a means one, as in a hundred being one hundred
read as round plus about: round says the number goes around, and about is circa, abbreviated as in dates

explanation.surface: A traffic roundabout from former times.
explanation.walkthrough: Roundabout does double duty: split into round, the container signal, and about, which gives C for circa.
explanation.definitionFit: Once means at some time in the past, a plain synonym of formerly in the sense of previously.

clue.text: Manager is mean to worker

parts.note: to mean to do something is to intend it
a worker ant, the commonest worker in cryptics

explanation.surface: A boss behaves nastily towards an employee.
explanation.walkthrough: Mean looks like an adjective for cruel, but it is the verb for having a purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: An intendant is an administrator or superintendent, especially the director of an opera house.

clue.text: Ridicule Tory leaving bait

indicators.note: the party member goes away, so those letters are taken out of the scorn word

parts.note: contempt is scornful ridicule
Con is short for Conservative, a Tory

explanation.surface: Mocking a departing Conservative who is the lure.
explanation.definitionFit: To bait someone is to tempt or lure them, as with food dangled on a hook.

clue.text: Terrible hunger initially: starve if it fails

definitions.text: Terrible hunger initially: starve if it fails

indicators.note: only the opening letter of hunger is taken

parts.note: hunger supplies only its opening letter

indicators.note: something terrible is in a bad state, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written: these six letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: When the crop fails, people go hungry and starve.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a failed crop means famine.
explanation.definitionFit: The harvest is the gathering of crops; if it fails, a whole community goes hungry.

clue.text: The two beginners duck twice around the moor

indicators.note: the two O's go around the other letters
twice means the duck's letter appears a second time

parts.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, O
L is a learner, a beginner, and there are two of them

explanation.surface: Two novices and a duck wander about on open moorland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The moor' suggests open heathland, but it means Shakespeare's Moor of Venice; a beginner is a learner, L.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello is the Moorish general in Shakespeare's play, so he is the moor.
